articles.title: Futures Trading, Explained: How Contracts, Margin and Leverage Really Work

articles.body:
Futures can give traders broad market exposure with a fraction of the contract’s full value upfront. That efficiency is their appeal—and the reason understanding margin, multipliers and risk is essential before placing a trade.

At its core, a futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price on a future date. The asset might be a stock index, crude oil, gold, Treasury bonds, a currency or an agricultural commodity.

Unlike buying shares, a trader generally does not pay the contract’s full notional value upfront. Instead, the broker requires margin: collateral that supports the position while gains and losses move through the account.

The contract multiplier changes everything

Consider the S&P 500 E-mini futures contract, known by its ticker ES. Assume ES is trading at 6,500 and carries a $50 multiplier.

Contract value = 6,500 × $50 = $325,000

One contract therefore controls $325,000 of market exposure. A trader does not necessarily deposit $325,000, but the profit and loss still reflect the full contract exposure.

If ES rises from 6,500 to 6,510, that is a 10-point move:

10 points × $50 = $500 profit

If ES falls 10 points, the same calculation produces a $500 loss.

> A futures trader may post only a fraction of the contract’s value, but gains and losses are calculated on the full exposure.

Long and short positions

LONG futures 📈
The position gains when the contract price rises and loses when it falls.

SHORT futures 📉
The position gains when the contract price falls and loses when it rises.

Futures markets are designed to accommodate either direction, which makes short exposure more straightforward than it can be in many stock accounts.

Margin is collateral—not the purchase price

Margin is often misunderstood. It is not a down payment that limits how much a trader can lose. It is collateral required by the broker or clearing system to keep the position open.

For example:

Contract exposure	Required margin	Exposure controlled
$325,000	Approximately $20,000	$325,000

The precise margin requirement varies by broker, contract and market volatility. When volatility increases, margin requirements can rise as well.

⚠️ A trader’s maximum loss is not limited to the initial margin deposit. In fast or adverse markets, losses can exceed the cash originally posted.

Daily settlement keeps risk moving

Futures positions are marked to market. Gains and losses are calculated as prices change and are settled through the trading account.

If losses push the account below required maintenance margin, the trader may need to add funds. If sufficient funds are not provided, the broker may reduce or liquidate the position.

Why futures exist

Futures serve two primary functions: hedging and speculation.

1. Hedging 🛡️
Businesses and investors use futures to reduce price risk. An airline may hedge against rising fuel costs, while a portfolio manager may use S&P 500 futures to reduce equity exposure without selling every stock in the portfolio.

2. Speculation 📊
Traders use futures to express a view on markets including:

S&P 500 — ES
Nasdaq-100 — NQ
Crude Oil — CL
Gold — GC
Treasury bonds
Agricultural commodities
Currencies

Micro futures offer smaller exposure

Micro contracts were created to provide smaller position sizes in popular markets. The Micro E-mini S&P 500 contract, or MES, uses a $5 multiplier—one-tenth of the ES multiplier.

Contract	Multiplier	P&L on a 10-point move
ES	$50	$500
MES	$5	$50

For a smaller account, MES can make position sizing more manageable. The risks of leverage still apply, but each point has a smaller dollar impact.

Futures and stocks are not the same

Feature	Stocks	Futures
Ownership	Own shares	Trade a contract
Expiration	Usually none	Yes
Leverage	Usually lower	Often high
Short exposure	Can involve restrictions	Relatively straightforward
Trading hours	Mostly regular market hours	Nearly 24 hours for many contracts
Margin	Depends on account and strategy	Core part of the product
Long-position loss potential	Generally limited to investment	Can exceed initial margin

The calculation every trader should know

Futures exposure can be summarized with one relationship:

Contract value = Futures price × Contract multiplier

Profit and loss follow a related formula:

P&L = Price movement × Contract multiplier × Number of contracts

For two MES contracts and a 20-point move:

+20 points × $5 × 2 contracts = +$200

A 20-point move in the opposite direction produces a $200 loss.

The bottom line

Futures are flexible tools for hedging, gaining market exposure and trading in either direction. But their efficiency comes from leverage, and leverage magnifies mistakes as quickly as it magnifies correct calls.

Before trading a futures contract, understand its multiplier, tick value, expiration, margin requirement and the maximum loss your account could reasonably absorb. Position size—not conviction—is what ultimately determines whether a trade is survivable.
